summaries.example: Imagine a group of rabbits living where the ground is often muddy. Some rabbits have fur that helps them blend in. If this difference can be passed to their babies, those rabbits may be harder for predators to spot. They may have more babies, and the helpful fur may become more common over many generations.
summaries.summary: Natural selection is a way populations can change over many generations. Members of a population vary. Some of their differences can be inherited. Because resources are limited and dangers exist, not every individual survives and has offspring. If an inherited trait helps an individual leave more descendants, that trait may become more common. The process can happen again and again, helping explain adaptations and the appearance of different species. The SEP entry also explains that “natural selection” can mean either the whole Darwinian process or one particular part of it. It asks whether selection must always produce visible evolutionary change, and whether selection is a real cause or sometimes only a way of describing patterns in data.
key_ideas: Natural selection needs differences among members of a population.
Some differences must be passed from parents to offspring.
Food, shelter, predators, disease, and weather limit how many individuals can survive and reproduce.
Over many generations, helpful inherited traits may become more common.
Philosophers use “natural selection” in two ways: sometimes for one part of the process, and sometimes for the whole repeating process.
A population can undergo selection even when one trait does not simply take over; several forms may remain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Natural selection helps explain how populations become well suited to their surroundings without needing to treat apparent design as proof of a special outside cause. It also teaches us to ask careful questions about evidence: Did a trait actually cause better reproduction, or did it merely happen to be found in individuals that had more offspring? These questions help distinguish a scientific explanation from a story that only sounds possible.

important_terms.definition: Differences among members of the same population, such as differences in body shape, color, or behavior.
The passing of a trait or pattern from parents to their offspring.
The process in which some inherited differences help their bearers survive and have more offspring than others.
A group of living things of the same kind living in an area and producing offspring.
A living thing’s success at surviving and producing offspring in a particular environment.

questions_to_think_about: Why would an inherited difference matter more in one environment than another?
Could a trait become common by chance rather than because it helped its bearers?
Can natural selection happen if a population stays fairly steady instead of changing in one direction?
What would scientists need to observe before saying that a trait helped reproduction?

summaries.example: Consider two alleles, A and a, in a population. Suppose organisms with two A copies, two a copies, or one of each have different reproductive success. In one model, fitness coefficients represent these differences and predict how allele frequencies change. If organisms with one A and one a have the highest fitness, both alleles may remain at a stable intermediate frequency rather than one replacing the other. Selection is still represented in the model even when directional change stops.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines natural selection as both a biological process and a philosophical concept. In the capacious sense, it refers to a repeating Darwinian process involving variation, inheritance or replication, and differences in survival or reproduction. In the focused sense, it refers to a particular component of a formal model, such as fitness variables in type recursions or a covariance term in the Price Equation. These interpretations are not automatically equivalent. The entry reviews attempts to state the conditions for evolution by natural selection, including Lewontin-style principles, and discusses objections involving population boundaries, counterexamples, inheritance, and covariance. It then considers replicator selectionism, which makes copying entities central, and asks whether evolution is required for selection. Stable polymorphisms suggest that selection can operate without one variant spreading to fixation. Finally, the entry addresses disputes over explanation and causation: selectionist accounts may be too speculative, circular, or model-dependent, while causal interpretations require specifying what fitness and drift represent.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes a focused conception of selection from a capacious conception that includes a full Darwinian cycle.
A common set of proposed conditions involves variation, differential reproductive success, and inheritance, but philosophers dispute whether these conditions are necessary or sufficient.

Replicator selectionism treats copying entities, especially genes, as central units of selection; critics argue that selection need not be limited to germ-line genes or to cases where copies are identical.
Selection need not produce directional evolution. Stabilizing selection can maintain a polymorphism, and selection can be offset by transmission effects or chance.
Type-recursion models and the Price Equation associate selection with different formal quantities, so they can give different descriptions of the same system.
Whether selection is a genuine cause, and what it can explain, depends partly on how models identify fitness, drift, inheritance, and causal relationships.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic shows why scientific theories need conceptual analysis as well as empirical evidence. “Natural selection” is not used in just one uncontested way, and formal models do not necessarily assign the word to the same quantity. Clarifying these choices affects what counts as selection, drift, inheritance, explanation, and cause. The discussion also encourages caution about adaptationist explanations: a trait’s usefulness may make a story plausible, but plausibility alone does not establish that selection caused the trait.

important_terms.definition: A broad usage of natural selection that includes a complete recurring process involving variation, inheritance or replication, and differential reproduction.
A narrower usage that identifies selection with one modeled contribution to evolutionary change, such as fitness coefficients or a covariance term.
An entity whose structure or information is copied, at least substantially, across successive generations or replication events.
A formal quantity representing how a type’s reproductive success affects population dynamics in a type-recursion model.
Random change associated with sampling and other chance influences, often modeled separately from focused selection.
A population pattern in which multiple variants persist at a relatively stable mixture rather than one variant becoming universal.
A statistical relationship between two variables; in the Price Equation, covariance between offspring number and phenotype is interpreted by some theorists as selection.
A relationship in which changing one factor would change another in the relevant model or system.

questions_to_think_about: Should a system count as undergoing natural selection if its population remains at an equilibrium? Why might the answer differ between a theory of selection and a theory of evolutionary change?
Are fitness differences causes of reproductive differences, summaries of those differences, or potentially either depending on the model?
How could a hitchhiking trait satisfy statistical conditions for selection without causing the increased reproduction itself?
What is gained and lost when selection is identified with fitness coefficients rather than with a covariance in the Price Equation?
What evidence would separate a well-supported selection explanation from a merely plausible adaptation story?

summaries.example: Suppose a school garden has two kinds of bean plants. One kind grows leaves that make it harder for insects to eat the plant. If the leaf pattern is inherited and the plants with it produce more seeds, that pattern may become more common in later generations. But imagine that plants with two different inherited forms do best together. Then both forms might remain in the garden. Selection could still be happening even though neither form completely takes over.
summaries.summary: Natural selection explains how inherited differences can affect the makeup of populations across generations. Because populations contain variation and resources are limited, individuals may leave different numbers of offspring. When reproductive differences are connected with inherited traits, those traits can spread or remain in changing proportions. Philosophers disagree about how to describe the process. Some use “natural selection” for the whole cycle; others use it for a particular factor in a mathematical model. The entry examines three-part proposals involving variation, fitness, and heredity, while noting that these proposals face counterexamples. It also discusses replicator selectionism, which gives special importance to entities that are copied, and the question of whether selection must always cause evolution. Stable mixtures of variants show that selection may help maintain a pattern rather than push one variant to replace all others. The entry further asks whether selection is a cause and whether selection explanations are supported by enough evidence.
key_ideas: Natural selection is discussed either as one part of evolutionary change or as the larger process containing variation, inheritance, and differential reproduction.
A widely discussed recipe for selection includes variation, different reproductive success, and heritable similarity, but philosophers have offered counterexamples and revisions.
The population being studied must be specified carefully; otherwise words such as selection and drift may be applied too loosely.
Replicator selectionism emphasizes entities that make copies, while other approaches focus on organisms, traits, or larger groups.
Selection can maintain several variants or be balanced by other processes, so evolution is not always a steady march toward one form.
Different mathematical models may disagree about which part of a process should be called selection.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding natural selection requires more than memorizing that “the strongest survive.” It requires asking which traits differ, whether the differences are inherited, what counts as success, and whether the trait caused the outcome or merely accompanied it. These distinctions help students understand why evolutionary explanations can be powerful while still needing careful models and evidence. They also explain why scientists and philosophers may use the same term in related but different ways.

important_terms.definition: Differences between individuals in a population that may affect how well they survive or reproduce.
The tendency for offspring to resemble their parents in relevant traits.
A process in which differences connected with survival or reproduction change the makeup of a population over generations.
A collection of organisms treated as a group for analyzing reproduction, inheritance, and change.
A measure or model of how successfully a type contributes offspring to later generations.
Change caused partly by chance sampling rather than by a trait’s effect on reproduction.
A copying entity, such as a gene in the standard example, that can leave descendants resembling it across replications.
A pattern in which several variants remain in a population over time.

questions_to_think_about: Does natural selection require a population to change noticeably from one generation to the next?
Why might a trait spread even if it is not itself the cause of greater reproduction?
How is chance different from selection in an explanation of population change?
Can a model be useful even if philosophers disagree about exactly what its terms mean?
What makes an explanation of an adaptation better than a story that is simply consistent with the adaptation?
